title: Checkpoint 0: Stockfish (skill 0) vs Hans
notes: Checkpoint after game 0, from the Queen's Gambit Declined: Hans plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: This is the classical Queen's Gambit Declined; White's 5.e3 invites normal development, and castling is the main line, keeping dxc4 and c6/Nbd7 options flexible. I checked that Bxf6 Bxf6 is harmless after castling, and cxd5 exd5 just gives a solid structure, so there are no tactics against me.

This is a Queen's Gambit Declined Exchange structure; recapturing with the pawn gives me a solid symmetrical pawn skeleton and frees my light-squared bishop's development via ...c6/...Nbd7 or ...Bf5 ideas. I checked 6...Nxd5 7.Bxe7 Qxe7 8.Nxd5 exd5, which is playable but gives White easy play; and 6...Qxd5 allows Bxf6 followed by Nxd5 tricks on the exposed queen.

Bxh3 just loses a piece to gxh3, so I'll develop instead; with White's h3 having cost a tempo, my light-squared bishop's natural outpost is f5, outside the pawn chain. If White tries 8.Nxd5 Nxd5 9.Bxe7 Nxe7 material stays level, and after 8.g4 Be6 White has only weakened his king.

White's Nge2 aims at Ng3 to harass my f5-bishop, so I want to finish development quickly and keep the option of ...c5 or ...c6. Nbd7 is solid: Bxf6 Nxf6 keeps d5 well guarded, and Nxd5 never works since Nxd5 just wins a piece, while ...Bxh3 would lose a bishop to gxh3.

White's g4 kicks my bishop, and grabbing the pawn (Bxg4 hxg4 Nxg4) just loses a piece for two pawns without a real attack, while Bg6 invites h4-h5 and f4-f5 harassment. Be6 keeps the bishop safe, reinforces d5, and prepares c5 to hit the centre while White's kingside pawn advances have loosened his own king.

White has committed to g4/h3 with the king still in the centre, so I want to trade off pieces and ease the pressure rather than grab the g4 pawn (10...Nxg4 11.hxg4 Bxg4 gives only two pawns for a knight). 10...Ne4 hits the Bg5 and the Nc3; after 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 12.Nxe4 dxe4 I'm comfortable with a solid structure, a fine bishop on e6, and the d5 square freed for my pieces.

I checked the g4 pawn carefully — h3 is gone after h4, the knight on e2 blocks the queen's d1–g4 diagonal, and nothing else covers g4, so Bxg4 simply snatches a pawn. The main try 12.Rg1 just costs a tempo (Bf5), and 12.Nxd5 fails to 12...Bxg5 13.hxg5 Qxd5 since d4 blocks the queen's defence of d5.

White's bishop on e7 must be recaptured, and the queen is the only piece that can do it, keeping my strong knight on e4 and the extra pawn from Bxg4. Alternatives like Nxf2 or Bxe2 just lose material or trade off my active pieces for nothing.

I'm a clean pawn up, but my e4 knight invites Nxe4 dxe4 Qxe4 regaining the pawn, so I resolve the tension first with Nxc3; note Qxh4 is a trap since Rh1 simply takes. After the recapture I keep a solid d5/c6 structure, an active bishop, and pressure on the loose h4 pawn.

My knight on c3 is attacked three times and undefended, so I must move it, and e4 is the ideal square since it's defended by the d5 pawn (and my queen) while only Qc2 attacks it. The alternative Nxa2 just trades my extra piece for a second pawn, whereas Ne4 keeps me a full knight ahead with a dominant centralized knight; if White grabs with Nxd5 I reply Qe6, hitting the knight and holding e4.

White's queen on e4 must be taken, and after the forced 16.Nxe4 I have the strong follow-up Bf3, hitting the undefended knight and the h1 rook at the same time, which should win material on top of my extra pawn. Recapturing with dxe4 instead would leave a loose pawn and allow annoying knight jumps like Nd5.

I'm a full queen ahead after White's blunder, so my only job is to move the attacked queen to safety while keeping things simple — Qxg2 and Qxf4/Qxe3+ all just lose the queen back to Nxg2/exf4/fxe3. Qxd4 is safe (Ne6 forking queen and rook fails to fxe6, and after Rd1 I have Qe5 defending d5), and it picks up a free central pawn while keeping my queen active.

I'm up a full queen for a knight, so the simplest path is to trade pieces and reduce White's attacking chances. My bishop on g4 is attacked by Bf3, so I take it; after Nxf3 hits my queen I'll just retreat it safely, and grabbing b2 instead would lose the bishop.

I'm up a bishop and two pawns, so safety and consolidation matter more than grabbing b2; note Qxf4 and Qxe3 both lose the queen since e3 and f2 cover each other. The bishop must move to a square the knight can't hit (Be2 and Bh5 drop it to Nxe2+/Nxh5, Bd1 to Rxd1), and Be4 is ideal: it's untouchable and shields the d5 pawn.

I'm up a queen and bishop for nothing, so I just need a safe, forcing continuation; Qxe3 grabs a pawn while hitting the undefended knight on f4, and d5 stays covered by my bishop. If White tries Nxd5 then Bxd5 simply wins the knight, and Rc3 or Rfe1 tricks all lose more material for White.

The knight on f4 is completely undefended — the f2 pawn doesn't cover it and Rf1 is blocked by that same pawn — so Qxf4 just wins a piece with no recapture. I avoided the tempting Qxc1, which loses the queen to Rxc1, and Qxf2+ only grabs a pawn.

I'm up a queen, bishop and knight for nothing, so I just need to grab material safely and avoid tactics; Qxh4 snags the free pawn while keeping my queen active near White's king. If White tries Rc5 to hit d5 I simply answer Nb6, after which the rook has no safe way to take.

White's f3 attacks my bishop, but Bxf3 immediately just loses it to Rxf3; instead Qg3+ forces Kh1 (f2, h2 and g2 are all covered, f1 is blocked by his own rook), and then Bxf3+ wins a rook since after Rxf3 I recapture with Qxf3+. That leaves me queen, knight and two rooks against a lone rook.

I'm up a queen and knight for a rook, and the f3 pawn is the only thing blocking my bishop's defence of g2 — Qg2 now would just be met by Kxg2. So I play Bxf3+, which is check with both king flights (g1, h2) covered by my queen, forcing Rxf3; then Qxf3+ leaves me queen and knight against a lone rook.

I'm overwhelmingly ahead in material, so the cleanest path is to simplify: Qxf3+ forces Rxf3 (king can't take, it's defended by nothing else and Kh1 can't reach), leaving me two rooks, a knight and seven pawns against a lone rook and two pawns. That removes all counterplay and tactical tricks.

I'm up a rook and a knight for nothing, so I just need safe activation rather than fireworks. Rae8 brings the idle rook to the open e-file with Re1+ ideas, and White's rook has no captures or checks in reply (Rxf7 is impossible since f7 is doubly defended).

I'm up two rooks and a knight for a rook, so the simplest path is to force simplification. Re1+ gives check; if White blocks with Rf1 I happily trade into a trivially winning rook+knight endgame, and otherwise after Kh2/Kg2 I can double rooks or hit the loose rook with Ne5.

I'm up a rook and a knight for two pawns, so the cleanest path is simplification: Rf1 attacks White's undefended rook on f3 and offers a trade that my other rook recaptures on, leaving an utterly trivial rook-and-knight-plus-seven-pawns win. If White declines with Rd3 or similar, I just trade or defend and push my extra material.

White's rook on f3 is completely undefended — my king on h2... rather White's king on h2 doesn't cover f3, so Rxf3 simply wins the rook outright. After 29.axb7 Rb8 I round up the pawn and win trivially with knight and five pawns versus one.

I'm up two rooks and a knight for nothing, so the only real concern is White's b7 pawn promoting; Rb8 blockades it permanently (and the knight on d7 even supports the rook there). After that White has only king moves and b4-b5, and I can bring the rooks around to mate at leisure, whereas hasty checks like Rf2+ allow Kg3 winning my rook.

White's only asset is the b7 pawn, and it's completely undefended since White has nothing but a king on g1 and a pawn on b4. Capturing with Rxb7 removes the last counterplay and leaves me two rooks and a knight up in a trivially winning endgame.

I noticed my rook on f3 is attacked by the white king on g2, so simply grabbing b4 with the other rook would cost a rook. Instead I move the f3-rook to b3, saving it while piling on the b4 pawn, which is undefended and will fall next move leaving White with a bare king.
I'm up two rooks and a knight against a lone king and the b4 pawn, so I just grab the last white pawn safely — the king on f1 can't touch my rook on b4. Then mating with two rooks is trivial.

I'm up two rooks and a knight against a bare king, so I just need a clean ladder mate. Rb2+ cuts the king off along the second rank: if Kf1 then Rb1# immediately, and if the king steps to the third rank I check with Rb3+ and walk him to the edge.

White has only a bare king, so I just need a ladder mate, but my b7 rook is boxed in on the 7th rank by my own pawns and knight, so it must come down the b-file. I'll slide the other rook to a2 to keep the king sealed on rank 1 (and far from capture), then deliver Rb1 mate next move.
My rook on a2 already cuts off the second rank, so dropping the other rook to b1 delivers back-rank mate — g1 is covered by the rook on b1 and g2/h2 by the rook on a2.
